beats: Your morning coffee is younger than a Greenland shark.
You see a shark as a fast predator in movies.
But deep beneath Arctic ice, the Greenland shark drifts in near‑freezing water.
Its muscles are saturated with urea and TMAO, natural antifreeze chemicals.
These compounds keep proteins stable, letting the heart beat once every eleven seconds.
Even blind from eye parasites, it relies on smell to locate sleeping seals.
So the animal that outlives nations may one day guide human heart therapies.
Your lifespan is a blink compared to a creature that has survived centuries of climate change.

beats: A Greenland shark swimming in the Arctic right now may have been born before the United States existed.
So how long has this longest‑lived vertebrate already been swimming in the Arctic?
Growing just a centimeter each year, it only reaches adulthood around 150 years old.
Its heart beats once every ten seconds, keeping it alive in –1°C water.
Muscles hold urea and TMAO, natural antifreeze against deep‑sea pressure.
Scientists radiocarbon-dated its eye lens proteins, formed before birth, to determine its age.
Thus a Greenland shark has already outlived nations, living around 400 years.
When you think of a century, remember that a single Greenland shark has already outlived nations.
